title: Dynamics of amorphous membranes in the two-dimensional limit
authors: Liga Jasulaneca, Alberto Martín-Pérez, Hongji Zhang, Prertahn Munireternam, Natalia A. Mamchik, Chee-Tat Toh, Artem K. Grebenko, Barbaros Özyilmaz, Makars Šiškins, Farbod Alijani
abstract: Atomically thin mechanical resonators have been realized predominantly in crystalline two-dimensional (2D) materials, such as graphene, where long-range crystalline order sets their elastic properties and defines their nonlinear resonant behavior. Extending these concepts to the amorphous 2D limit has remained largely unexplored. Here, we demonstrate that monolayer amorphous carbon (MAC) forms suspended membranes that support optothermal actuation and sensitive interferometric readout across both linear and nonlinear regimes of its resonant motion. We resolve thermomechanical motion, driven resonances, and multimode spectra in MAC nanodrums. The frequencies of fundamental vibration modes correspond to unusually low pretensions, placing monolayer MAC nanodrums in a regime where geometric nonlinearities, stress heterogeneity, and mode coupling emerge at comparatively low drive powers. Consistently, we observe pronounced nonlinear dynamics, including hardening, softening, and mixed Duffing responses, nonlinear damping, parametrically excited modes, and signatures of intermodal coupling. These results establish MAC as a robust nanoelectromechanical platform and open an experimental route to disorder-governed nanomechanics in the 2D amorphous limit.
summary: This work demonstrates that amorphous carbon (MAC) membranes can function as highly sensitive nanoelectromechanical resonators, opening a new platform for studying mechanics governed by structural disorder. By analyzing nonlinear resonance features like Duffing responses and mode coupling, the authors establish MAC's utility for investigating complex dynamics in the 2D amorphous limit.
main_problem: The study aims to extend mechanical resonator research from crystalline 2D materials (like graphene) to the amorphous 2D limit using monolayer amorphous carbon (MAC). This explores how structural disorder affects nanoscale mechanics.
main_result: MAC membranes are established as a robust nanoelectromechanical platform, exhibiting pronounced nonlinear dynamics including hardening/softening and intermodal coupling at low effective pretension.
method: The research combines optothermal actuation with sensitive interferometric readout to characterize the mechanical resonance and nonlinear response of suspended MAC nanodrums.
model_or_system: The physical system is atomically thin, amorphous carbon (MAC) membranes suspended over substrates. The analysis models the dynamics using a tensioned membrane description and incorporates optical transduction via reflection from the air-membrane-vacuum gap stack.
key_observables: Resonant frequencies ($\sim 13.9$ MHz), Quality factors ($Q$), nonlinear Duffing responses (hardening/softening), and mode spectra showing intermodal coupling.
important_parameters: Low effective pretension regime ($10^{-4} - 10^{-3} 	ext{ N m}^{-1}$), which amplifies geometric nonlinearities and stress heterogeneity effects.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on a transfer-matrix model for optical reflection and assumes the system can be described by modified Duffing oscillator equations, though deviations suggest more complex coupling.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate structural characterization (Raman/AFM), linear dynamic response spectra showing $Q$ distribution, and mode spectra demonstrating nonlinear behavior like internal resonance dips.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the physical platform (MAC membranes) to characterizing its fundamental linear dynamics, then delving into complex nonlinear regimes by analyzing frequency-response curves and multi-mode spectral signatures.
why_interesting: While focused on classical mechanics, the study of disorder-governed dynamics, nonlinearity, and mode coupling in low-dimensional systems provides experimental analogs for understanding dissipation and emergent behavior in open quantum systems or disordered many-body models.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Optothermal actuation and interferometric readout of vibrating monolayer amorphous carbon (MAC) membranes. (a) Schematic illustration of MAC, highlighting its structural characteristics: five-, six-, seven-, and eight-member rings, varying bond angles and lengths, and locally hexagonal patches. (b) Raman spectrum acquired on suspended monolayer MAC, showing the disorder-activated D band near 1340 cm−1 and the G band near 1588 cm−1, consistent with disordered sp2 carbon. (c) SEM image of MAC suspended over a Si-supported holey SiNx array, showing continuous suspended regions across the circular openings. (d) AFM characterization of transferred MAC. FIG. 2. Linear dynamic response of monolayer MAC nan- odrums. (a) Power spectrum showing a Lorentzian-shaped resonance from which a fundamental frequency of 13.9 MHz and Qth = 843 ± 24 were obtained. (b) Driven fundamental mode of the same nanodrum, with f0,driven ≈13.6 MHz and Qdriven = 302 ± 27. (c) Q distribution for MAC nanodrums with radius R = 1.25 µm and 2.50 µm. (d) Pretension dis- tributions for the same radius values. Horizontal and vertical black bars indicate the median values and interquartile ranges of n0 and Q. Data points are slightly scattered in radius value for clarity.

FIG. 3. Amplitude-dependent nonlinear dynamics of MAC resonators. Near-resonant driven responses showing hardening (a) and softening (c) Duffing-type nonlinearities with increasing blue laser drive power. (b, d) Nonlinear damping, indicated by the quadratic relationship between the drive and maximum response amplitudes. Dashed and solid lines show linear and quadratic fits, respectively. (e) Transition from hardening (H) to mixed (M) to softening (S) in a representative MAC nanodrum and (f) statistics of nanodrums showing different nonlinear response types.

FIG. 4. Signatures of modal interactions in a MAC nan- odrum. (a) Frequency response at increasing drive, showing the development of a dip in the resonance peak amplitude, consistent with the onset of internal resonance. (b) The same response plotted in normalized units, Vout/Vin, highlights the strong reduction in the apparent quality factor Q. (c) Mode spectrum of a similar MAC nanodrum, showing secondary mode near 2f0, suggesting a 2:1 internal resonance.

FIG. 5. Mode spectra of monolayer and multilayer MAC nanodrums. Representative spectra of (a) monolayer and (b) multilayer MAC nanodrums show multiple vibrational modes and nonlinear response features. Thin vertical lines are guides to the eye marking the mode-frequency ratios expected for an ideal tension-dominated circular membrane.
